doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Tallmadge's fieldwork in black and white churches
summary: Mancuso describes Tallmadge's background and how he took him to holiness churches, where he would play gospel and win over the congregations.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: You know, I was Chaz with Jazz. That’s what I believed too. But you know, through Tallmadge, Bill was this amazing, gentle, tall, bland-looking Nebraskan guy, you know? But he had been on the road with the bubble guy.

Lawrence Welk. And Lawrence Welk, that’s when he had a little bit of a jazz group. And Bill played some jazzy stuff with him, you know. I don’t think he recorded. But, so when he did his studies, you know, he really started with hymnody, white hymnody, and shaped-notes singing, and spirituals and Gospels with blacks. And then he was big on folk music, you know, the Song Catchers and all that. This was a side I didn’t know about. So he would take me to Springville. I mean I’m a West Side kid you know. We’d go to Springville and we’d go looking for these records. And we would go to these holiness churches and he’d take me to black churches and white churches and when he’d take me to a black church, everybody’s black. And here comes this pale, tall man. And I had some trepidation, you know, but I guess he knows some of these people. And they’d open the door and we’d go walking in and they’re pounding the tambourines and everything and they’d go, “Professor Tallmadge is here.” It was a white man who teaches at the university center who thinks what we do is significant. Was that something. And they froze. They’d go “Oh Professor Tallmadge, how are you doing?” “Oh fine.” You know, he didn’t talk real loud or anything. And he said, “Would you play something for us?” And he’d sit down and he’d play a Gospel tune and they just went crazy because this white guy, who looked so square, could do this stuff. And I was astounded. Because I really couldn’t play it or anything. I mean I eventually took some piano lessons.
Could you join in from even just a clapping your hands —
And did you feel compelled to do so, because of the music? I mean —
No, not to show them that I could do off-beat stuff.

No I was so respectful. I’d stay out of the way. Because he was the show. I was just a sidekick. They didn’t know who I was and they didn’t really care. They figured I probably was his son. So I was an adjunct to him. He was the one. When we went into some of the white churches the same kind of thing happened. And so I learned all this stuff because of Bill.
